(d) Some visitors believe the Mayan system is a true base-20 system and read the third level as 400s. The museum will put a warning sign beside the one numeral that such a visitor misreads by the most. Which numeral gets the sign? Justify with numbers.
questions.a: (a) 3 x 20 + 10 = 70. (b) 1 x 360 + 1 x 20 + 0 = 380; the shell shows that the 1s level is empty, so the dots are read as one 360 and one 20, not as 20 + 1. (c) 7 x 360 + 0 x 20 + 19 = 2520 + 19 = 2539. (d) Numeral P. Q has no third level, so the visitor reads it correctly as 70. R would be read as 400 + 20 = 420, off by 40. P would be read as 7 x 400 + 19 = 2819, off by 7 x 40 = 280, the largest error, because the error is 40 for every unit on the third level.
s: Part (a): 70
Part (b): 380, with the shell marking the empty 1s level
Part (c): 2539
Part (d): P, misread by 280, against 40 for R and none for Q

questions.q: In a base-2 place value system that uses the word ukasar for the digit 1 and urapon for the digit 0, which number is written 'ukasar urapon ukasar ukasar'?
Raghav says: 'The Indian zero did the same job as the Mesopotamian placeholder, and no more.' Check his claim.
questions.a: Partly right. Like the Mesopotamian placeholder, the Indian 0 marks an empty position, and unlike it, it is used at the end of a numeral too. But in Indian mathematics 0 was also a number in its own right: Aryabhata used its arithmetic properties (0 added to a number leaves it the same, 0 times any number is 0) in 499 CE, and Brahmagupta codified 0 as a number in 628 CE. So 'no more' is wrong.
s: Agrees that the Indian 0 also works as a placeholder
Explains that 0 was also treated as a number, with Aryabhata's or Brahmagupta's use
Gives the verdict: partly right

questions.q:
In Chinese rod numerals the units, hundreds and ten-thousands are written in zong form and the tens and thousands in heng form; an empty place is left blank.
(a) For the number 52013, say which form each digit is written in and where the blank goes.
(b) Why does alternating the two forms make a rod numeral easier to read?
questions.a: (a) 5 (ten-thousands) in zong form, 2 (thousands) in heng form, a blank for the hundreds, 1 (tens) in heng form and 3 (units) in zong form. (b) Neighbouring places are written in different forms, so a reader can tell where one digit ends and the next begins, and can tell the places apart even without careful spacing.
s: Part (a): zong 5, heng 2, blank hundreds, heng 1, zong 3
Part (b): neighbouring digits look different, so the places can be told apart

questions.q:
A merchant records the amount 7203 in three systems: the Mesopotamian base-60 system (using a placeholder in the middle of a numeral, as the later Mesopotamians did), the Egyptian system and the Hindu system.
(a) Group 7203 into powers of 60 and write the Mesopotamian groups, showing where the placeholder is needed.
(b) How many symbols does the Egyptian numeral for 7203 use?
(c) His next amount is 7200. Explain the trouble a Mesopotamian scribe would have writing it, and how the Hindu numeral avoids it.
(d) Suppose the Hindu numerals have not yet reached the merchant, so he must choose between the Egyptian and the Mesopotamian systems. He cares most that no numeral can ever be misread, even if it takes more symbols. Which should he choose? Justify using 7203 and 7200.
questions.a: (a) 7203 = (2) x 3600 + (0) x 60 + 3, so (2) (placeholder) (3): the placeholder marks the empty 60s position. (b) 7 symbols for 1000, 2 for 100 and 3 strokes: 12 symbols. (c) 7200 = (2) x 3600 + 0 x 60 + 0, so both lower positions are empty. The placeholder was used mainly in the middle and not at the end, so the numeral could look like plain (2), which is 2. The Hindu numeral 7200 writes 0 in both empty places, so it can be read only one way. (d) The Egyptian system. Every Egyptian symbol carries its own landmark number, so 7203 (12 symbols) and 7200 (9 symbols) can each be read in only one way, wherever the symbols stand. The Mesopotamian numerals are shorter, but 7200 could be misread as 2, which breaks his main condition.
s: Part (a): (2) (placeholder) (3)
Part (b): 12 symbols
Part (c): 7200 could look like 2 without end placeholders; the Hindu 0 removes this
Part (d): Egyptian, because its symbols cannot be misread, though longer than the Mesopotamian numerals

questions.q:
Form a base-2 place value system using the word ukasar for the digit 1 and urapon for the digit 0.
(a) Write the first five landmark numbers (positions) of base 2.
(b) Write 6 in this system.
(c) Write 13 in this system.
(d) How many words does 13 take here, and how many in the Gumulgal way of counting in twos carried past 6 (ukasar for 2, urapon for 1, added up)?
(e) The Gumulgal had to call every number above 6 ras. Explain why this base-2 system never needs such a word.
questions.a: (a) 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. (b) 6 = 1 x 4 + 1 x 2 + 0 x 1: ukasar ukasar urapon. (c) 13 = 1 x 8 + 1 x 4 + 0 x 2 + 1 x 1: ukasar ukasar urapon ukasar. (d) 4 words here; the Gumulgal-style name is ukasar said 6 times and urapon, 7 words. (e) Here the words are digits whose position gives their value, so a new position can always be added for the next power of 2 and any number can be written with just two words; the Gumulgal names simply added up 2s and 1s, so they grew longer and longer, and the Gumulgal stopped naming after 6.
s: Part (b): ukasar ukasar urapon
Part (c): ukasar ukasar urapon ukasar
Part (d): 4 words against 7
Part (e): explains that place value lets two digits write any number
